newsitem.title: USA: Frigid cold, snow curbs U.S. feed usage, shipments.
newsitem.headline: Frigid cold, snow curbs U.S. feed usage, shipments.

text.p: U.S. feed companies reported a slowdown in livestock feed usage and shipments during the latest spell of frigid cold and snow and doubt they will recover that lost volume when the weather warms up.
Cattle eat less during periods of frigid cold, livestock experts said because they huddle away from the feedbunks.
"The reduction of the intake is far more dramatic than the increase once the cattle resume normal eating patterns," said Gerry Kuhl, an Kansas State University extension feedlot specialist.
Officials with several railroad companies told Reuters earlier this week that snow in the upper Midwest and northern Great Plains slowed traffic on the rails but that the situation was improving.
Layne Anderson, vice president for Golden Sun Feeds in Estherville, Iowa, said there were shipping delays in the Dakotas, Minnesota and northern Iowa, with the severest problems in South Dakota.
"South Dakota is just an absolute disaster," he said.
Once the frigid weather abates, Anderson expects pent-up demand for feed.
Once the wind and cold subside, Kuhl said cattle consumption quickly returns to normal.
Also, blizzard conditions and sub-zero temperatures have severely curbed truck deliveries, feed dealers said.

One problem encountered by feed dealers during this frigid cold spell was with transportation. Huge snow drifts in Minnesota and the Dakotas have closed roads, while sub-zero weather in the Dakotas and across much of Midwest has caused diesel fuel to coagulate, halting feed trucks.
"In general, we are backing up loads. We've got ingredients that can't get there," a Minneapolis dealer said.
"When we do get back to nicer weather, we expect to be awfully busy," he said.
Milder Midwest weather was forecast this weekend, with high temperatures in the 20's Fahrenheit.

Feed dealers said prices for ingredients such as millfeeds and soybean meal have slipped this past week largely due to shipping problems and reduced feed intake by cattle. Hog consumption has not been severely affected because most hogs are raised in large barns and shielded from the cold.
Shipping delays extended as far east as Indiana where snow and cold made highways treacherous.
"It has kind of paralyzed us here right now," said an Indiana dealer. "The trucks have totally stopped."
